Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claims 1, 5, 6, 8, 10  are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US Patent 10,626,523 to Lim in view of US Patent 9,544,945 to Hadoulias.
In Reference to Claim 1
Lim discloses a dryer appliance defining a vertical direction, a lateral direction, and a transverse direction, the dryer appliance comprising: a cabinet (Fig. 6, 26); a drum (Fig. 6, 28) rotatably mounted within the cabinet, the drum defining a chamber for receipt of clothes for drying and a chamber inlet; an inlet duct (Fig. 6, 52) fluidly coupled to the chamber inlet; an air handler (Fig. 6, 32) in fluid communication with the inlet duct for urging a flow of air through the inlet duct and into the chamber; and an induction heating assembly in thermal communication with the inlet duct, the induction heating assembly comprising: an induction coil (Fig. 6, 110) for generating an electromagnetic field; a heating plate (Fig. 6, 112) for generating heat when energized by the electromagnetic field;
Lim does not teach a heat exchanger.
Hadoulias teaches a heat exchanger (Fig. 1, 105) in conductive thermal communication with the heating plate.
It would have been obvious to one with ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, to incorporate teachings from Hadoulias into the design of Lim.  Doing so, would result in a heat exchanger being implemented into the inlet duct of Lim.  Both inventions of Lim and Hadoulias having conductive heating system for an air dryer, Hadoulias teaches  a high efficiency process to supply heat to heated air (Col. 1, Line 45-50)

Lim teaches the heating plate (Fig. 6, 112) is positioned outside of the inlet duct.
Lim does not teach the heat exchanger.
the heat exchanger comprises a plurality of fins (As showed in Fig. 6) oriented generally along the direction of the flow of air urged through the inlet duct by the air handler.
Hadoulias teaches the heat exchangers is positioned within the inlet duct (As showed in Fig. 1)
It would have been obvious to one with ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, to incorporate teachings from Hadoulias into the design of Lim.  Doing so, would result in a heat exchanger being implemented into the inlet duct of Lim.  Both inventions of Lim and Hadoulias having conductive heating system for an air dryer, Hadoulias teaches  a high efficiency process to supply heat to heated air (Col. 1, Line 45-50)

Lim does not teach a heat exchanger in the air duct.
Hadoulias teaches the heat exchanger comprises a flow conditioner plate ( heat exchanger can use both a combination of induction heated substrates that are ferrous or magnetic in various configurations) a ferritic material

Claims 2-4, 7 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over the combination of Lim and Hadoulias as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of US Patent Publication 2017/0247831 to Hayes.
In Reference to Claims 2-4
Lim discloses the heating plate  (Fig. 6, 112) comprises a first material which is a ferritic material (Col. 6, Line 10-15)
The combination of Lim and Hadoulia as applied to Claim 1 does not teach the material of heat exchanger.
Hayes teaches the heat exchanger having aluminum fins (Paragraph 65)
It would have been obvious to one with ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, to incorporate teachings from Hayes into the combination of Lim and Hadoulia as applied to Claim 1.  Doing so, would result in the heat exchanger including aluminum fins.  Both inventions of Lim and Hayes are for cloth dryer with heated air, Hayes teaches an heat exchanger design with an increased surface of exchanger (Paragraph 65)

Doing so, would result in the heat exchanger including aluminum fins.  Both inventions of Lim and Hayes are for cloth dryer with heated air, Hayes teaches an heat exchanger design with an increased surface of exchanger (Paragraph 65)

In Reference to Claim 9
Lim teach the coil.
The combination of Lim and Hadonlias as applied to Claim 1 does not teach the coil wound around the inlet duct.
Espin teaches the induction coil is wound around an outside of the inlet duct (As showed in Fig. 1)
It would have been obvious to one with ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, to incorporate teachings from Espin into the combination of Lim and Hadonlias as applied to Claim1. Both inventions of Lim and Espin have a pipe for delivering working media, and the working media being heated by external heater.  Espin teaches a method of enabling the material to be heated more efficiently, since the contact area has been increased.
